hints.content:
The slope of the tangent line at a point is equal to $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ at that point. In the case of polar curves, we can use the relationship:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{\left( \dfrac{dy}{d\theta} \right)}{\left( \dfrac{dx}{d\theta} \right)}$

For a polar curve, $x=\goldE{r}\cos(\theta)$ and $y=\goldE{r}\sin(\theta)$. Therefore, in our problem we have:

$\begin{align}
x&=\goldE{\tan(\theta)}\cos(\theta)
\\\\
y&=\goldE{\tan(\theta)} \sin(\theta)
\end{align}$

options.explanation:
$\begin{align}
y(\theta)&={\tan(\theta)}\sin(\theta)
\\\\
\dfrac{dy}{d\theta}&=\sec^2(\theta)\sin(\theta)+\tan(\theta)\cos(\theta)
\\\\
&=\sec^2(\theta)\sin(\theta)+\sin(\theta)
\\\\
\\\\
x(\theta)&={\tan(\theta)}\cos(\theta)
\\\\
&=\dfrac{\sin(\theta)}{\cos(\theta)}\cdot\cos(\theta)
\\\\
&=\sin(\theta)
\\\\
\dfrac{dx}{d\theta}&=\cos(\theta)
\end{align}$

Note: Because we are only interested in the derivative when $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, we knew that $\cos(\theta)\neq 0$ and were able to cancel it.
